title: “Ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath” — the Greek has “ten yoke of oxen” and “a jar”
summary: In the KJV, “ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath”, a measure of liquid. In Brenton’s Greek the land is ploughed by ten yoke of oxen (δέκα ζεύγη βοῶν) and yields one κεράμιον, a jar; the sower’s six artabas yield three measures. The KJV states a vineyard; the Greek names no vineyard in this clause.
text: KJV Isaiah 5:10: “Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 5:10: כִּ֗י עֲשֶׂ֙רֶת֙ צִמְדֵּי־כֶ֔רֶם יַעֲשׂ֖וּ בַּ֣ת אֶחָ֑ת וְזֶ֥רַע חֹ֖מֶר יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה אֵיפָֽה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 5:10: Οὗ γὰρ ἐργῶνται δέκα ζεύγη βοῶν, ποιήσει κεράμιον ἕν· καὶ ὁ σπείρων ἀρτάβας ἓξ, ποιήσει μέτρα τρία. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA05.htm.
reasoning: The KJV and the Greek both give a small yield from a large input, but the first input differs. The KJV says “acres of vineyard”; the Greek says “yoke of oxen”, the team that ploughs a field. The Hebrew צִמְדֵּי־כֶרֶם is “yokes of vineyard”, usually taken as a land measure, the area a yoke of oxen works, which the KJV renders “acres”. The Greek has the yoke of oxen and drops “vineyard”. The second clause also differs in the measure: KJV “seed of an homer … an ephah”, Greek “six artabas … three measures”.
scope: T applies at 5:10 only, and to the first clause and the measures. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together. “Acre” in the KJV is a rendering of a Hebrew word for a yoke of land, so the KJV and the Hebrew do not disagree here. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and this record compares the wording of the texts and does not show which reading is original.

title: “From Hamath, and from the islands of the sea” — the Greek has “from the rising of the sun, and from Arabia”
summary: The KJV lists places from which the Lord recovers the remnant: Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath and the islands of the sea. Brenton’s Greek lists Assyrians, Egypt, Babylonia, Ethiopia, the Elamites, “the rising of the sun” (ἡλίου ἀνατολῶν) and Arabia. The last two items differ from the KJV’s last two.
text: KJV Isaiah 11:11: “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 11:11: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בַּיֹּ֣ום הַה֗וּא יֹוסִ֨יף אֲדֹנָ֤י ׀ שֵׁנִית֙ יָדֹ֔ו לִקְנֹ֖ות אֶת־שְׁאָ֣ר עַמֹּ֑ו אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִשָּׁאֵר֩ מֵאַשּׁ֨וּר וּמִמִּצְרַ֜יִם וּמִפַּתְרֹ֣וס וּמִכּ֗וּשׁ וּמֵעֵילָ֤ם וּמִשִּׁנְעָר֙ וּמֵ֣חֲמָ֔ת וּמֵאִיֵּ֖י הַיָּֽם׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 11:11: Καὶ ἔσται τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, προσθήσει ὁ Κύριος τοῦ δεῖξαι τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ, τοῦ ζηλῶσαι τὸ καταλειφθὲν ὑπόλοιπον τοῦ λαοῦ, ὃ ἂν καταλειφθῇ ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀσσυρίων, καὶ ἀπὸ Αἰγύπτου, καὶ ἀπὸ Βαβυλωνίας, καὶ ἀπὸ Αἰθιοπίας, καὶ ἀπὸ Ἐλαμιτῶν, καὶ ἀπὸ ἡλίου ἀνατολῶν, καὶ ἐξ Ἀραβίας. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA11.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew ends with וּמֵחֲמָת וּמֵאִיֵּי הַיָּם, “and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea”. The Greek has no Hamath and no islands in the same slot; it has “from the rising of the sun” and “from Arabia”. Pathros and Shinar are named in the KJV and not in the Greek (the Greek has Babylonia where the KJV has Shinar). Only the last two items are the subject of this record.

title: “The golden city ceased” — the Greek has “the taskmaster has ceased”
summary: In the KJV the proverb against the king of Babylon says “How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!” Brenton’s Greek reads “How has the exactor (ὁ ἀπαιτῶν) ceased, and the taskmaster (ὁ ἐπισπουδαστής) ceased?” where the KJV has “the golden city”.
text: KJV Isaiah 14:4: “That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 14:4: וְנָשָׂ֜אתָ הַמָּשָׁ֥ל הַזֶּ֛ה עַל־מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל וְאָמָ֑רְתָּ אֵ֚יךְ שָׁבַ֣ת נֹגֵ֔שׂ שָׁבְתָ֖ה מַדְהֵבָֽה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 14:4: Καὶ λήψῃ τὸν θρῆνον τοῦτον ἐπὶ τὸν βασιλέα Βαβυλῶνος, Πῶς ἀναπέπαυται ὁ ἀπαιτῶν, καὶ ἀναπέπαυται ὁ ἐπισπουδαστής; Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/14/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA14.htm.
reasoning: The first half of the line agrees: a person who exacts or oppresses has ceased. The second half differs in kind. The KJV has a place, “the golden city”. The Greek has a second person who drives or presses others, a title parallel to the first. The Hebrew word is מַדְהֵבָה, which occurs only here; the KJV takes it as a golden place and the Greek as a person.
scope: T applies at 14:4, second clause, only. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say what מַדְהֵבָה means. The Hebrew is a word that occurs once, so it cannot be checked against other uses in the same book. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon” and “lions upon him that escapeth of Moab” — the Greek reads differently in both
summary: In the KJV, Moab “is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep” (15:2), and the Lord says “I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land” (15:9). Brenton’s Greek has “Debon, where your altar is” (οὗ ὁ βωμὸς ὑμῶν) at 15:2, and “I will bring Arabians upon Deimon, and I will take away the seed of Moab, and Ariel, and the remnant of Adama” at 15:9.
text: KJV Isaiah 15:2: “He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off.” KJV Isaiah 15:9: “For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 15:2: עָלָ֨ה הַבַּ֧יִת וְדִיבֹ֛ן הַבָּמֹ֖ות לְבֶ֑כִי עַל־נְבֹ֞ו וְעַ֤ל מֵֽידְבָא֙ מֹואָ֣ב יְיֵלִ֔יל בְּכָל־רֹאשָׁ֣יו קָרְחָ֔ה כָּל־זָקָ֖ן גְּרוּעָֽה׃ Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 15:9: כִּ֣י מֵ֤י דִימֹון֙ מָ֣לְאוּ דָ֔ם כִּֽי־אָשִׁ֥ית עַל־דִּימֹ֖ון נֹוסָפֹ֑ות לִפְלֵיטַ֤ת מֹואָב֙ אַרְיֵ֔ה וְלִשְׁאֵרִ֖ית אֲדָמָֽה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 15:2: Λυπεῖσθε ἐφʼ ἑαυτοὺς, ἀπολεῖται γὰρ καὶ Δηβὼν, οὗ ὁ βωμὸς ὑμῶν· ἐκεῖ ἀναβήσεσθε κλαίειν, ἐπὶ Ναβαῦ τῆς Μωαβίτιδος· ὀλολύξατε, ἐπὶ πάσης κεφαλῆς φαλάκρωμα, πάντες βραχίονες κατατετμημένοι. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 15:9: Τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ τὸ Δειμὼν πλησθήσεται αἵματος, ἐπάξω γὰρ ἐπὶ Δειμὼν Ἄραβας, καὶ ἀρῶ τὸ σπέρμα Μωὰβ, καὶ Ἀριὴλ, καὶ τὸ κατάλοιπον Ἄδαμὰ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/15/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA15.htm.
reasoning: At 15:2 the Hebrew הַבַּיִת is “the house” with the article; the KJV takes it as the place name Bajith and the Greek has no such place, and gives “where your altar is”, a place of worship. At 15:9 the Hebrew has נוֹסָפוֹת (“more”) and אַרְיֵה, a lion, which the KJV renders “more” and “lions”; the Greek has “Arabians” in the first slot and “Ariel” in the second, and ends with Adama as a place name where the KJV has “the land” (אֲדָמָה). In both verses the Greek names a worshipping place or people where the KJV has either a place name or an animal.

The KJV spells the same place as “Dibon” at 15:2 and “Dimon” at 15:9 because the Hebrew spellings differ; that is not tagged separately. text: KJV Isaiah 16:1: “Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 16:1: שִׁלְחוּ־כַ֥ר מֹשֵֽׁל־אֶ֖רֶץ מִסֶּ֣לַע מִדְבָּ֑רָה אֶל־הַ֖ר בַּת־צִיֹּֽון׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 16:1: Ἀποστέλω ὡς ἑρπετὰ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν· μὴ πέτρα ἔρημός ἐστι τὸ ὄρος θυγατρὸς Σιών; Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/16/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA16.htm.

title: “A forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch” — the Greek has “the Amorites and the Hivites” who deserted their cities
summary: The KJV compares Israel’s strong cities to “a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel”. Brenton’s Greek says the cities will be deserted “as the Amorites and the Hivites (Εὐαῖοι) deserted theirs from before the sons of Israel”.
text: KJV Isaiah 17:9: “In that day shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 17:9: בַּיֹּ֨ום הַה֜וּא יִהְי֣וּ ׀ עָרֵ֣י מָעֻזֹּ֗ו כַּעֲזוּבַ֤ת הַחֹ֙רֶשׁ֙ וְהָ֣אָמִ֔יר אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָזְב֔וּ מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְהָיְתָ֖ה שְׁמָמָֽה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 17:9: Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἔσονται αἱ πόλεις σου ἐγκαταλελειμμέναι, ὃν τρόπον κατέλιπον οἱ Ἀμοῤῥαῖοι καὶ οἱ Εὐαῖοι ἀπὸ προσώπου τῶν νἱῶν Ἰσραήλ· καὶ ἔσονται ἔρημοι, Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/17/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA17.htm.

The Hebrew words and the names are not spelled alike, and this record does not explain how the Greek reading arose.

title: “The moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed” — the Greek has “the brick shall melt, and the wall fall”
summary: In the KJV, when the Lord reigns in Zion “the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed”. Brenton’s Greek has Καὶ τακήσεται ἡ πλίνθος, καὶ πεσεῖται τὸ τεῖχος, “and the brick shall melt, and the wall shall fall”, where the KJV has moon and sun.
text: KJV Isaiah 24:23: “Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 24:23: וְחָֽפְרָה֙ הַלְּבָנָ֔ה וּבֹושָׁ֖ה הַֽחַמָּ֑ה כִּֽי־מָלַ֞ךְ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָאֹ֗ות בְּהַ֤ר צִיֹּון֙ וּבִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְנֶ֥גֶד זְקֵנָ֖יו כָּבֹֽוד׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 24:23: Καὶ τακήσεται ἡ πλίνθος, καὶ πεσεῖται τὸ τεῖχος· ὅτι βασιλεύσει Κύριος ἐκ Σιὼν, καὶ ἐξ Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ ἐνώπιον τῶν πρεσβυτέρων δοξασθήσεται. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/24/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA24.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has הַלְּבָנָה, “the white one”, the usual poetic word for the moon, and הַחַמָּה, “the hot one”, the sun. The Greek has the nouns for brick (πλίνθος) and wall (τεῖχος). In unpointed Hebrew the word for the moon (לבנה) has the same consonants as the word for a brick (לְבֵנָה), and the word for the sun (חמה) is close to the word for a wall (חומה). The KJV reads the heavenly bodies and the Greek reads building materials. The result is two different pictures at the moment of the Lord’s reign.
scope: T applies at 24:23, first clause, only; the rest of the verse (the Lord reigning in Zion and Jerusalem before his ancients) is close. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The comparison of the Hebrew nouns with “brick” and “wall” is made from the consonants and is for the reader to weigh; the record does not say the Greek translator used another Hebrew text. summary: In Hezekiah’s writing the KJV has “I shall not see the Lord, even the Lord, in the land of the living”. Brenton’s Greek reads Εἶπα, οὐκέτι οὐ μὴ ἴδω τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπὶ γῆς ζώντων, οὐκέτι μὴ ἴδω τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ Ἰσραήλ — “I shall no more see the salvation of God … I shall no more see the salvation of Israel”.

title: “For Isaiah had said” and “Hezekiah also had said” — the Hebrew has “And Isaiah said” and “And Hezekiah said”
summary: The KJV of Isaiah 38:21–22 puts the two speeches in the past perfect: “For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs … Hezekiah also had said, What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?” The Hebrew has וַיֹּאמֶר יְשַׁעְיָהוּ and וַיֹּאמֶר חִזְקִיָּהוּ, “And Isaiah said … And Hezekiah said”, with no “for” and no “had”. Brenton’s Greek has Καὶ εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας … Καὶ εἶπεν Ἐζεκίας, the plain past.
text: KJV Isaiah 38:21: “For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover.” KJV Isaiah 38:22: “Hezekiah also had said, What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 38:21: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְשַׁעְיָ֔הוּ יִשְׂא֖וּ דְּבֶ֣לֶת תְּאֵנִ֑ים וְיִמְרְח֥וּ עַֽל־הַשְּׁחִ֖ין וְיֶֽחִי׃ Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 38:22: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ מָ֣ה אֹ֑ות כִּ֥י אֶעֱלֶ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 38:21: Καὶ εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας πρὸς Ἐζεκίαν, λάβε παλάθην ἐκ σύκων, καὶ τρίψον, καὶ κατάπλασαι, καὶ ὑγιὴς ἔσῃ. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 38:22: Καὶ εἶπεν Ἐζεκίας, τοῦτο σημεῖον πρὸς Ἐζεκίαν, ὅτι ἀναβήσομαι εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/38/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA38.htm.
reasoning: In 2 Kings 20:7–8 the same two speeches stand in order: Isaiah calls for the figs and Hezekiah afterwards asks for the sign. In Isaiah 38 they stand last, after the sign (38:7–8) and Hezekiah’s writing. The KJV’s “had said” turns the last two verses into a look back to events already narrated, which removes the difference of order. The Hebrew and the Greek do not carry a look back; the verbs read as the plain past. (Brenton’s English of the Greek also says “had said”, but that is its translator’s English; the Greek is καὶ εἶπεν.)
scope: T applies at 38:21–22 only. The difference found is between the KJV and the Hebrew and Greek. The English past perfect can be a fair way to render a Hebrew narrative tense that follows an earlier event, so the KJV reading is possible; the record says only that the Hebrew and the Greek carry no “had” and no “for”. The record does not say that the order in Isaiah 38 is the order in which the events happened. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and this record compares the wording of the texts and does not show which reading is original.

text: KJV Isaiah 52:15: “So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 52:15: כֵּ֤ן יַזֶּה֙ גֹּויִ֣ם רַבִּ֔ים עָלָ֛יו יִקְפְּצ֥וּ מְלָכִ֖ים פִּיהֶ֑ם כִּ֠י אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא־סֻפַּ֤ר לָהֶם֙ רָא֔וּ וַאֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־שָׁמְע֖וּ הִתְבֹּונָֽנוּ׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 52:15: Οὕτω θαυμάσονται ἔθνη πολλὰ ἐπʼ αὐτῷ, καὶ συνέξουσι βασιλεῖς τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν· ὅτι οἷς οὐκ ἀνηγγέλη περὶ αὐτοῦ, ὄψονται, καὶ οἳ οὐκ ἀκηκόασι, συνήσουσι. title: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man” — the Greek has “the transgressor that sacrifices a calf is as he that kills a dog”
summary: The KJV compares a worshipper’s sacrifice with a crime: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog’s neck.” Brenton’s Greek has Ὁ δὲ ἄνομος ὁ θύων μοι μόσχον, ὡς ὁ ἀποκτέννων κύνα — “The lawless one who sacrifices a calf to me is as one who kills a dog” — with a single transgressor and one pair of acts.
text: KJV Isaiah 66:3: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog's neck; he that offereth an oblation, as if he offered swine's blood; he that burneth incense, as if he blessed an idol. Yea, they have chosen their own ways, and their soul delighteth in their abominations.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 66:3: שֹׁוחֵ֨ט הַשֹּׁ֜ור מַכֵּה־אִ֗ישׁ זֹובֵ֤חַ הַשֶּׂה֙ עֹ֣רֵֽף כֶּ֔לֶב מַעֲלֵ֤ה מִנְחָה֙ דַּם־חֲזִ֔יר מַזְכִּ֥יר לְבֹנָ֖ה מְבָ֣רֵֽךְ אָ֑וֶן גַּם־הֵ֗מָּה בָּֽחֲרוּ֙ בְּדַרְכֵיהֶ֔ם וּבְשִׁקּוּצֵיהֶ֖ם נַפְשָׁ֥ם חָפֵֽצָה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Isaiah 66:3: Ὁ δὲ ἄνομος ὁ θύων μοι μόσχον, ὡς ὁ ἀποκτέννων κύνα· ὁ δὲ ἀναφέρων σεμίδαλιν, ὡς αἷμα ὕειον· ὁ διδοὺς λίβανον εἰς μνημόσυνον, ὡς βλάσφημος. Καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐξελέξαντο τὰς ὁδοὺς αὐτῶν, καὶ τὰ βδελύγματα αὐτῶν ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτῶν ἠθέλησε. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/66/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA66.htm.

title: “Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow” — the Greek has “Phud, and Lud, and Mosoch”
